topic: The Collision-Pi Connection: Why Bouncing Blocks Compute Pi
target_audience: High school physics students and undergraduate mathematics enthusiasts

sections.title: The Strange Setup: A Counting Mystery
sections.content: Introduce the physical system: a frictionless floor, a fixed wall on the left, a small block (mass m), and a large block (mass M) sliding in from the right. We count every 'clack' (collision) between blocks and between the small block and the wall.
sections.example: Visualize a tiny hamster in a small box (1kg) and a massive elephant in a large box (100kg) sliding toward each other. When the elephant hits the hamster, and the hamster hits the wall, we count the total bounces.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Laws of the Game
sections.content: Explain perfectly elastic collisions using two fundamental laws: Conservation of Momentum (mass times velocity) and Conservation of Energy (kinetic energy). These two equations define how the velocities change after every hit.
sections.example: Graphical overlay showing the equations: m*v1 + M*v2 = Constant (Momentum) and 1/2*m*v1^2 + 1/2*M*v2^2 = Total Energy.

sections.title: The Pattern Emerges: Scaling the Mass
sections.content: Show what happens when we increase the mass ratio in powers of 100. If M = 1kg and m = 1kg, we get 3 collisions. If M = 100kg, we get 31 collisions. If M = 10,000kg, we get 314 collisions.
sections.example: An animation showing the 'clacks' speeding up as the mass ratio increases. 1:1 ratio -> 3 clacks; 1:100 ratio -> 31 clacks; 1:1,000,000 ratio -> 3,141 clacks. The digits of Pi appear!

sections.title: The Geometry of Velocity: Mapping to a Circle
sections.content: Transform the physics into geometry. By rescaling the velocity axes (using the square root of the masses), the Conservation of Energy equation becomes the equation of a circle: x² + y² = R². Every collision is a jump from one point on the circle to another.
sections.example: A coordinate system where the x-axis is 'Velocity of small block' and the y-axis is 'Velocity of big block'. As collisions occur, a point traces steps around the perimeter of a circle.

sections.title: The Angle of Pi: Why the Counting Works
sections.content: Explain that each collision corresponds to a fixed-size arc on the circle. The total number of collisions is the number of times this arc fits into the semi-circle (Pi radians). As the big block's mass increases, the arc angle becomes smaller, allowing for more precise 'steps' along the curve.
sections.example: A visual showing a circle being 'sliced' into tiny even pieces. The number of pieces represents the number of collisions. The total length of the 'path' is exactly Pi.

sections.title: Conclusion: Physics as a Computer
sections.content: Summarize how a simple physical interaction acts as a mechanical computer for calculating one of the most fundamental constants in mathematics. Emphasize the beauty of how disparate fields like dynamics and geometry intersect.
sections.example: A final shot of the blocks hitting 3,141,592 times as the mass ratio becomes astronomical, with the symbol π glowing in the background.
